slides.title: Our 2025 baseline is 21.0bn litres, with road use accounting for most demand
slides.takeaway: Petrol: 8.86bn L. Diesel: 12.13bn L. Total demand falls from 21.94bn L in 2023 to an estimated 20.99bn L in 2025.
slides.source: Department sales through 2023; energy balances and Stats SA activity; Eskom/IPP evidence. All 2025 segment allocations are estimates; other diesel retains an explicit residual.

slides.title: Demand stays broadly flat in our base case; supply and routes determine where imports enter
rows: Eskom fuel fell from 1.13bn L in FY2024 to 0.68bn in FY2025
Power demand reduction: 0.54bn L; includes assumed private backup
7.5% road-freight shift to rail; 1% annual road-fuel efficiency gain
Rail saves 0.33bn L; road efficiency saves 0.79bn L
5.8bn L directed planning baseline; no restart in base case
Demand-implied gross imports remain about 16.6bn L in 2030
Existing Matola infrastructure and an assumed 0.20bn L additional SA flow
Imports change gateway; national fuel demand stays unchanged
slides.takeaway: Activity adds 1.54bn L by 2030, broadly offsetting power, efficiency and rail reductions. Customer access determines Vopak capture.
slides.source: 2025 analytical workbook v02: registered demand assumptions and user-directed 5.8bn L domestic production case. Estimates are not reported actuals.

slides.title: Petrol has declined since 2013, while diesel has sustained the market
side: 2024–25 are estimates; 2013–23 use one consistent Department series.
slides.takeaway: Petrol remains below its earlier level; diesel demand responds more directly to freight, industry and power.
slides.source: Department annual sales, 2013–2023. Estimated 2024–2025: analytical workbook v02. Earlier deck FIASA comparison figures are not spliced into this series.

slides.title: Road use dominates the baseline, with meaningful diesel demand outside transport
side: Other diesel: 1.91bn L remains unallocated to a specific end use.
slides.takeaway: Sector-attributed vehicle fuel stays in its sector; the road split is an explicit allocation assumption.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Segments. 2021 energy-balance road volume; 75% of road diesel allocated to freight. Historical sector intensities at current activity.

slides.title: Agricultural demand rebounds in 2025 while mining and manufacturing remain broadly flat
side: Manufacturing covers the energy-balance industry residual, not a complete industrial census.
slides.takeaway: Sector activity produces different demand paths; applying one GDP growth rate would hide these differences.
slides.source: Stats SA mining/manufacturing indices and agriculture real GVA; mean 2018–2021 fuel intensity. Sector diesel values after 2021 are estimates.

slides.title: Efficiency offsets activity growth in the petrol baseline
rows: A combined efficiency / fleet-mix assumption reduces fuel per unit of activity
Compounding activity and intensity yields a modest decline
Applied after activity growth; rail displacement is then applied to freight only
slides.takeaway: The assumptions are explicit and editable; EV uptake is not counted again as a separate reduction.
slides.source: Department 2023 sales; analytical workbook v02, Assumptions and Demand history. Activity and efficiency settings are authored planning assumptions.

slides.title: Eskom fuel use fell by about 40% in FY2025 as supply performance improved
side: The utility series includes kerosene. Fiscal years end in March.
slides.takeaway: The demand baseline replaces annual power consumption explicitly, so the decline is not hidden in a generic growth rate.
slides.source: Eskom Integrated Report 2025 p141; staged source series. 679.1m L diesel + kerosene supersedes the earlier slide’s 677.9m figure for this scope.

slides.title: Further power recovery removes 0.54bn litres in the 2030 base case
rows: Eskom FY proxy, IPP generation conversion and private backup
Separate from reported Eskom fuel; not a measured national census
Recovery persists across utility and backup requirements
High-import case retains power use; low-import case retains 35%
slides.takeaway: Power demand can fall without an equivalent decline in transport or industrial demand.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Segments / Driver bridge. Private backup 2023/24/25: 0.8/0.6/0.2bn L. IPP conversion: 0.31 L/kWh. FY-to-calendar and fuel-mix assumptions apply.

slides.title: Road still carries most reported freight despite the recent recovery in rail volumes
side: Tonnes measure payload, not tonne-kilometres or directly displaced diesel.
slides.takeaway: Rail recovery changes fuel demand through eligible freight, distance, truck efficiency and the rail traction mix.
slides.source: Stats SA P7162 December 2025 p7; all reported freight. Analytical workbook v02, Evidence.

slides.title: A 7.5% shift of road-freight activity to rail saves 0.33bn litres in the base case
slides.takeaway: These shifts apply to road-freight activity, not the entire diesel market; sector demand and power remain separate.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Driver bridge and scenario assumptions. Shift interpreted as freight tonne-km share. Distances and eligibility remain assumed; cases also vary growth and efficiency.

slides.title: The 5.8bn-litre production assumption leaves a gross import requirement of about 16.7bn litres
slides.takeaway: 5.8bn litres sets the planning case. Aggregate closure does not validate domestic output or its petrol/diesel split.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Balance and Supply assumption. User direction 11 October 2026. Original plant-based estimate 10.23bn L retained in appendix.

slides.title: Refinery recovery is the largest downside risk to the import requirement
rows: 15% increase in the national planning volume
Assumed 2029 start; 65% utilisation after a two-year ramp
Assumed 2029 start; 50% utilisation after a two-year ramp
slides.takeaway: Restart dates and ramp-up settings are scenario assumptions. Import-terminal operations can compete before refining resumes.
slides.source: Registered scenario assumptions; DR08 refinery evidence. Capacity inputs: SAPREF 180kb/d, PetroSA 45kb/d; 70% petrol/diesel yield in restart sensitivities. Dates are not project commitments.

slides.title: Base-case imports remain near 16.6bn litres; refinery recovery creates a much lower outcome
side: Cases are sensitivities, not assigned probabilities.
slides.takeaway: The base case balances activity growth against efficiency, rail and power reductions; supply assumptions drive the widest spread.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Scenarios. Demand-implied gross imports = demand − domestic supply + 2025 exports. Zero stock change; 5.8bn L directed opening supply.

slides.title: Matola provides an existing alternative gateway; new gas projects have a different role
headers: Implication for South African fuel routes
rows: Broader storage base; product allocation and overlap need confirmation
Regional supply; no additional SA flow assigned in the base case
Light oil, gas and LPG; production began December 2025
No direct finished petrol/diesel output credited
Current cross-border flow is far smaller than gross storage suggests
slides.takeaway: Storage capacity, berth capacity and delivered South African volumes measure different things and are not added together.
slides.source: Galp Matola announcement (3 Dec 2020); Petromoc logistics; Sasol Mozambique operations; SARS customs. URLs retained in notes / workbook.

slides.title: Matola needs a landed-price or service advantage to offset border and logistics costs
rows: 600km one way; round trip; R25/truck-km; 40,000L payload
550km one way; terminal and border costs; one-day delay
Required landed-product discount under these illustrative costs
About 15 additional loaded trucks/day over 330 days
slides.takeaway: Mozambique diversion changes the gateway serving demand. It does not reduce South Africa’s national import requirement.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Mozambique. Distances, tariffs, border charges, financing and allocation are authored sensitivities, not carrier quotes or confirmed access.

slides.title: Vopak’s capture depends on the accessible share of Durban imports
rows: Gateway proxy before customer and route allocation
20% of Durban gateway volume; no contracted share inferred
50% of captured Durban flow; counted within the same fuel volume
slides.takeaway: The illustrative unique flow is 2.63bn litres. Adding Lesedi would double-count fuel handled at both sites.
slides.source: Registered market_review.yaml and market_review.json, 10 October. Capture is total conditional flow, not incremental sales; domestic and other-terminal Lesedi receipts are outside this screen.

slides.title: The illustrative capture case fits the tank-turn screen, making usable capacity the next test
rows: 124,000m³ working capacity, partly estimated; two turns/month
Receipt, product segregation, dispatch, pipeline access and peak demand
slides.takeaway: Working-tank arithmetic screens feasibility. Engineering limits and current customer flows determine actual headroom.
slides.source: Registered terminal_site_assumptions.csv and market_review.json. Durban working subset is not the full terminal; access, peaks and current throughput remain open.

slides.title: The market supports an import platform; customer capture and capacity constraints govern investment
rows: Prioritise identifiable customer segments and destinations
About 16.6bn litres in 2030 under the 5.8bn supply case
Plan for ongoing imports; retain refinery sensitivities
Gateways compete for the same fuel
Mozambique base diversion of 0.20bn L is a route assumption
Validate delivered cost, service and customer access
Illustrative 2.63bn L unique flow fits the tank-turn screen
Secure additional volumes, prove the bottleneck, then compare improvement and expansion returns
slides.takeaway: Next decisions: review the product balance, obtain route quotes and customer commitments, and establish usable capacity at both sites.
slides.source: 2025 analytical workbook v02: registered demand assumptions and user-directed 5.8bn L domestic production case. Estimates are not reported actuals.

slides.title: The national supply assumption closes the total balance but leaves the product mix unresolved
slides.takeaway: The 5.8bn L override uses the original estimated production mix. Offsetting product differences remain visible; no product allocation is claimed as verified.
slides.source: Analytical workbook v02, Supply assumption and Balance. Original plant estimate: Secunda 3.95, Natref 2.37, Astron 3.91bn L; 10.23bn total. These do not govern the directed case.
